title: Who Made "Zhang Shichao, Where Did You Put My House Keys?" — and That "Absolutely Superior Feeling"
excerpt: This choir showed people that choral singing could mean more than red songs and folk standards like *Yellow River Cantata* and *Jasmine Flower*. It could mean Japanese-style songs like *Sunset Glow* and *Bamboo Grove*, and a choir could take them to the stage.
body:
This choir showed people that choral singing could mean more than red songs and folk standards like *Yellow River Cantata* and *Jasmine Flower*. It could mean Japanese-style songs like *Sunset Glow* and *Bamboo Grove*, and a choir could take them to the stage.

Ever since *Zhang Shichao, Where Did You Put My House Keys?* became the first viral hit of 2016, Jin Chengzhi's phone has not stopped ringing. Even a man who installs security doors tracked him down: "Teacher Jin! I can fit you an electronic door you never need keys for. You open it with a phone app!"

In the five-plus years since its formal founding, this amateur chamber choir had never been courted like this.

Jin Chengzhi founded the Rainbow Chamber Choir in 2010. A group of conducting students wanted to keep singing together after a choir competition, and the choir grew out of that. It expanded almost entirely through friends introducing friends, and now has 40 members. They come from every walk of life: programmers, teachers, foreign-company employees, full-time mothers. Eighty percent are not professional musicians. Many are students, so rehearsals follow the school semester, usually once a week; any more often and people couldn't find the time.

Because rehearsal time is short, the choir stages only two concerts of new repertoire a year. On July 11, 2015, it held [*Voices of Summer: An Evening of Japanese Works*](http://music.163.com/#/album?id=3442649), singing familiar songs such as *Castle in the Sky* and *Princess Mononoke* from [Hayao Miyazaki's films](http://music.163.com/#/song?id=41462817). The attention it got amounted to a few enthusiastic audience members tagging the choir's official Weibo account and reports from two or three media outlets.

That, of course, is nothing like the treatment a viral hit gets.

You may have heard *Zhang Shichao, Where Did You Put My House Keys?* It has sat near the top of NetEase Cloud Music's new-song chart for days. When the music starts, your first impression may be "classical," the kind you hear in a school auditorium. Then the lyrics make you wonder whether you're listening to it the right way. That strange contrast is the main charm of a song that complains about a roommate too busy dating to care whether anyone else lives or dies.

In Jin Chengzhi's words, it gives you an "absolutely superior feeling."

![Jin Chengzhi, founder and conductor of the Rainbow Chamber Choir](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702130125qBHzeyZrIs5bKQDw.jpg-w600)

Jin Chengzhi is 29, yet the members call him "Old Jin." He wrote the viral hit *Zhang Shichao, Where Did You Put My House Keys?*

Old Jin is an entertaining man. At rehearsal he tells those who aren't singing well enough: "What's wrong with you, haven't had your energy drink?!" Sometimes he scolds a member on purpose, then wheels out her birthday cake while she stands there at a loss. Adding a kazoo, an instrument that sounds inherently comic, to *Zhang Shichao* was also his idea.

To understand the choir's style, look at the scores, which Jin Chengzhi designs almost entirely himself. Open the score book *A Tale of Two Cities*: past a blue-green cover made to look like a thread-bound book, the first thing you see is a landscape painting printed with the choir's motto, "Follow Nature's Course, Be Sincere in Elegance." It suits that sense of "elegance" well. Turn a few more pages, though, and a selfie of Jin Chengzhi appears. His goofy face beside a modern oil painting breaks the mood at once.

Where the score would normally carry musical directions such as "gently" or "lightly," Jin Chengzhi has written his own: "absolutely superior feeling," "confident and showing off," "superior feeling intensifying," and finally "blow the audience away." Across the title of the piece *The Old Man Who Carried Firewood*, comic-book lettering asks: "A perfect comeback?"

![A page from a Rainbow Chamber Choir score with Jin Chengzhi's handwritten-style directions](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607261507461H4bJtnoevWCFZw2.jpg-w600)

The Jin Chengzhi selfie, which has reportedly appeared in every score since 2013, is there mainly to keep members from getting too nervous in rehearsal or on stage. The "absolutely superior feelings" help members grasp the emotion Jin Chengzhi wants the music to carry.

"These terms were translated from Italian into a common international language and then into Chinese, so there are two layers in between," says Li Jiacheng, a tenor. "When Teacher Jin writes it this way, it's intuitive and easy to understand."

In fact, Jin Chengzhi is a man who pursues "elegance." He trained in classical music and likes to study Middle Chinese and Japanese haiku. The keynote he set for the Rainbow choir is "elegance" too.

His early works, *Jingguang Mountain Morning* and *Yumen Pass*, are grand in scale. His more recent collections, *A Tale of Two Cities* and *Zeya Collection*, are full of relaxed, fresh pieces such as [*Sunset Glow*](http://music.163.com/#/song?id=41602916) and [*Moon-Viewing Pavilion*](http://music.163.com/#/song?id=41602915). Jin Chengzhi says this "elegant" style comes from Zeya Mountain in Wenzhou. While his father was recovering from an illness, the family spent a pleasant, idyllic stretch of time there. The fishing, the cooking fires, the hillsides and streams in the lyrics are things he lived himself. He put those scenes into *Zeya Collection*, and one of its pieces, [*Bamboo Grove*](http://music.163.com/#/song?id=41602914), is sung in the Wenzhou dialect.

Jin Chengzhi no longer tries, as he did early on, to tell a story through music with a beginning, an end and plenty of twists. He now asks that each piece be "one emotion, one image, one musical language." He admires the standard that Matsuo Basho, the master of haiku, set for the form. *Moon-Viewing Pavilion*, for instance, is simply a picture of watching the moon from a pavilion while a bamboo grove sways gently: no purpose, no moral, only an image.

This is the man who wrote *Zhang Shichao, Where Did You Put My House Keys?* and then had everyone sing it with full solemnity. For Jin Chengzhi, turning funny things that happen among friends into songs is dessert after a big meal. It is fun, but it is not the main course.

"Take away the word 'elegance' and I'll fight you to the death!" he says.

![The Rainbow Chamber Choir performing](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702130126Q0HPzvJoUZ7f8b2i.jpg-w600)

Jin Chengzhi's style has shaped the Rainbow choir he directs, and it has become the choir's biggest draw. Many people who had sung in official choirs, at school or elsewhere, never knew a choir could sing this kind of music: not just red songs and folk standards like *Yellow River Cantata* and *Jasmine Flower*, but Japanese-style songs like *Sunset Glow* and *Bamboo Grove*, and take them to the stage.

Li Jiacheng felt exactly that. In May 2015 he came to the Rainbow Chamber Choir only because a friend told him to give it a try. He planned to hang around for a week and quit; instead he discovered that "a choir can sing these works." The July concert was close by then. Bit by bit he wrote romanized pronunciation over every piece, and he often went to Jin Chengzhi's home for one-on-one vocal coaching. When he finally went on stage he was elated. "I wasn't nervous at all, and when we finished I didn't want to leave the stage."

The concerts are thrilling, and they are one of the two big events of the choir's year. As soon as one concert ends, the venue for the same time next year has to be booked. Eight months out, planning of the repertoire begins. Six months out, the scores are prepared and printed. In the last four months, once the new semester starts, rehearsals begin, along with work on publicity such as posters and copy.

At that point the fixed date works like a deadline, a tool for pushing members to improve. Those who miss too many rehearsals face an extra assessment before they can go on stage. "The biggest punishment is of course not being allowed on stage, but we try to get every member who comes to rehearsals onto the stage. We insist on strict attendance so members understand that the choir is a team, and any one person's absence slows everyone's progress," says deputy leader Chen Jia, who handles attendance, personnel and other internal matters. Perfect attendance is rewarded: this year with things like power banks and seals.

The members have long since grown used to Jin Chengzhi's style. When he says at rehearsal, "It feels like only the parts of you above the neck are alive," everyone knows exactly what he means. Cracking up and trading jibes between run-throughs is routine, but once they get serious, they can laugh their way through *Zhang Shichao* once and then sing it with complete earnestness.

Jin Chengzhi brings a strong personal style to the other choirs he coaches too, but Rainbow is still where he gets along best with the members.

That probably explains why so many people love this choir. In Jin Chengzhi's words, it is a "family."

The rehearsal runs three hours every Monday evening, from 6 to 9 p.m., and some people skip work or classes to be there. One member travels every week from Songjiang to the rehearsal site in Xuhui District, 30 kilometers away, and catches the last metro home. "Attendance gets better every year. Unless something urgent comes up, like a company business trip out of town, they all come. Even with a fever they come and sit at the back and listen," Jin Chengzhi says. The membership has also settled down. In earlier years a handful of people left after every concert. Over the two concerts from the middle of last year to this year, only one or two left each time, mostly for reasons they couldn't avoid, such as going abroad to study.

![Rainbow Chamber Choir members at rehearsal](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160726150747Zq8Q2vVG4iSEWKdx.jpg-w600)

But for an amateur choir like Rainbow, raising money is hard.

Hong Chuan, artistic director of Fudan University's Echo Chamber Choir, told this reporter that choirs fall roughly into three kinds. The first signs labor contracts with its singers and lives on commercial performances; that kind exists basically only abroad. The second belongs to an institution or organization, such as a school choir or a company union choir. The third, like Echo and Rainbow, is an amateur choir formed purely by people who love choral singing. Such choirs usually operate as registered student clubs under a school, as Echo does at Fudan and Rainbow does at the Shanghai Conservatory of Music.

Choirs like these rarely earn money, and they spend little. They usually rehearse in idle music classrooms borrowed from the school. During winter and summer breaks, when the campus is closed, any extra rehearsal means begging someone for a room.

Often Rainbow's members can't gather to rehearse, so Jin Chengzhi has them come to his home for individual vocal coaching. Each week he assigns choral homework. Members record their parts with a recording app and send them to their section leaders to check.

To attract new members, Hong Chuan believes, a concert is the best advertisement. Both he and Jin Chengzhi say applications surge after each concert. A week after the *A Tale of Two Cities* concert, *Zhang Shichao* went viral, and the Rainbow choir suddenly received nearly 200 applications, almost four times the number in a regular recruitment round.

A normal round takes about 10 new members. Accurate pitch and the ability to read music are the basic requirements; choral experience doesn't matter. Jin Chengzhi will tell you which muscle in your throat to move and how, rather than, like some music teachers, simply having you imitate his voice or piling on jargon such as "Don't put the sound so far forward, place it further back." "I have Hong Chuan to thank for that. I learned it from him," Jin Chengzhi says.

Jin Chengzhi knows Hong Chuan well; in fact, everyone in their circle knows everyone else. They often get together to drink and talk about music and running a choir, and sometimes help each other out, lending a conductor or singers for a joint performance. Hong Chuan says that for amateur choirs like Echo and Rainbow, the concert is both the biggest expense and the biggest source of income each year.

Renting the He Luting Concert Hall, Rainbow's "home ground," costs about 30,000 yuan a booking, and ticket sales barely cover the rent and the cost of staging the concert. Beyond that, private donations and side events such as lectures bring some money into the choir's fund, which pays for perfect-attendance rewards, regular group dinners and birthday celebrations. Often the two conductors, Jin Chengzhi and Hong Chuan, also put the money they earn conducting elsewhere back into their own choirs.

Jin Chengzhi's day job is conducting and rehearsing groups all over the region. Besides Rainbow's fixed Monday-evening rehearsal, he now spends one week rehearsing groups in Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Shanghai and elsewhere, and the next giving small vocal lessons at home to Rainbow members, trying to reach every member within that week. His family doesn't really understand, because he has let Rainbow reshape his own life plans. In 2013 he intended to study in Europe, but he couldn't find a suitable conductor to entrust the choir to. Hiring a conductor on the open market costs several thousand yuan for two hours, which an amateur choir with no fixed income simply can't pay. So in the end he stayed.

"I want to protect what they love," Jin Chengzhi says. "They," of course, includes himself. He knows his parents can't understand this. It is a difference in values: the older generation cares more about making a living, while people like him, as long as they can get by, will chase what they love. "I keep trying to persuade them. Maybe they understand a little more now."

![Male members of the Rainbow Chamber Choir in sunglasses on stage](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160726150747syYXDkt4wbe85lfH.jpg-w600)

*"**When all the guys in the choir put on sunglasses, I knew Teacher Jin was going to show off big time.**" A comment under the song on NetEase Cloud Music from user Nemo294840653*

*Zhang Shichao* has taken off, but Jin Chengzhi wants the Rainbow choir to stay as it is: a choir of amateur singers who sing as professionally as they can. He is extremely wary of the word "commercialization." He doesn't want the choir caught up in money disputes, which he believes are the only thing that could break it up.

"Everyone came to this choir out of love for choral singing, and everyone has a day job," Jin Chengzhi says. If the choir took on too many performances, its current level of training would not be up to it. "If extra rehearsals got in the way of members' jobs, that's a responsibility I couldn't bear. I have to make sure they can work in peace."

On the evening of January 18, the Rainbow Chamber Choir added a last-minute rehearsal because a company had asked to film a documentary. The venue, a meeting room in a church, had been borrowed through a contact that same day. More than ten media outlets crammed into the small room with cameras of every size, and the shutters clicked nonstop while the choir sang. Operations director Xu Shiyu stood by the door greeting people as they came and went, fielding all kinds of questions and lining up interviews for after rehearsal; whenever she found a spare moment, she sang a passage softly along with the rest of the choir.

In fact, Jin Chengzhi's expectations are modest. Given how Chinese audiences currently listen and live, he says, Rainbow could never tour on a large scale the way foreign choirs do. After *A Tale of Two Cities*, he wrote an afterword that makes one request: that parents who let their kids run wild please turn off their phones.
